children: , the enterprise-software and cloud-computing giant, published a draft code of conduct for its internally developed AI models as the industry wrestles with how far frontier systems should be allowed to go. Shares traded at $499.27 Tuesday, with the latest valuation snapshot showing Microsoft below its estimated GF Value. The timing is notable: investors are no longer watching only how quickly Microsoft can build more capable AI, but also how tightly the company can control the technology as spending continues to climb.

Microsoft's 37-page framework says its AI systems should remain under human authority, including accepting correction, interruption and shutdown. The draft also rejects giving AI systems legal personhood or encouraging them to imitate consciousness. Microsoft is opening the framework to a six-week consultation before producing a revised version intended to influence model development in 2027 and beyond. Importantly, the company also makes clear that its existing models were not trained using the new code and that written rules alone cannot guarantee how an AI system will behave.

That leaves investors with a simple but expensive question: can Microsoft keep pushing the AI frontier without turning safety controls into a brake on commercial performance? The valuation picture gives that debate another layer. Microsoft's $499.27 share price sits 14.62% below the $584.75 GF Value estimate shown in the chart, suggesting the stock is trading below GuruFocus' estimate of fair value. With Microsoft generating roughly $90 billion in quarterly revenue and pouring almost $10 billion into research and development, the payoff will depend on whether those billions create AI products that are both powerful enough to win customers and controlled enough to earn their trust.

title: Microsoft Slips After Drawing a Line Around Its Own AI
